title: Validation Gets Tested At 1kW
gist: As AI accelerators reach kilowatt-class power, engineers from Advantest, Synopsys, Nordson, Modus Test, NLM Photonics, Teradyne and proteanTecs describe validation expanding far beyond fault coverage to include thermal, spatial, workload and time-domain coverage, because the test hardware itself (contacts, sockets, load boards, coolers) now becomes part of the reliability problem and OSATs cannot realistically burn-in devices long enough to prove long-run reliability.

insights.claim: At kilowatt-class power, two different AI accelerator workloads can hold the same total power level while stressing entirely different compute blocks, memory interfaces, and power-delivery paths, meaning a single peak-power spec says nothing about where heat actually concentrates on the die.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Power-spec-based qualification alone is no longer sufficient; investors evaluating AI chip reliability claims should ask vendors about workload-level thermal mapping, not just peak-wattage specs.
insights.quote: two workloads can hold an AI accelerator at the same power level while driving different compute blocks, memory interfaces, and power-delivery paths
insights.locator: On a spec sheet, 1kW of maximum power

insights.claim: Synopsys says engineers must stop assuming worst-case power at a given temperature is sufficient sign-off criteria, and must instead know exactly where the 1,000 watts are spatially distributed across the die, because the aggregate power number alone is meaningless for reliability.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signals rising demand for chip-level thermal/power simulation tools as AI accelerator sign-off criteria tighten, a growth data point for Synopsys.
insights.quote: The engineer has to stop assuming that worst-case power at this temperature is the criterion to safely sign off on a chip,
insights.locator: That pushes validation beyond aggregate limits

insights.claim: Synopsys says spreadsheet-based power/thermal analysis is no longer adequate; engineers must run the real design against real workload stimulus and measure temperature everywhere to generate the data needed to back up system design quality claims.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Another concrete signal of rising EDA simulation/measurement tool spend tied to AI accelerator power scaling.
insights.quote: You’re going to use your real design, run the workload, give the stimulus, and measure temperature everywhere. You have to have data to back up your system design quality.
insights.locator: Today, a spreadsheet is not enough

themes.theme: Test Hardware Becomes Part Of The Reliability Problem

insights.claim: Advantest says fault coverage alone is no longer sufficient for AI accelerator validation; engineers now must correlate fault coverage with thermal coverage together, since a test can exercise the correct logic without reproducing the heat distribution of a real workload.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signals ATE vendors need combined electrical-plus-thermal test capability, a product differentiation lever for Advantest and Teradyne in the AI accelerator test market.
insights.quote: We normally look at fault coverage, but now we have to start thinking about correlating fault coverage with thermal coverage. We can’t just look at fault coverage alone. We have to look at fault coverage and thermal coverage collectively.
insights.locator: This is a new trend in AI

insights.claim: Nordson says that at kilowatt-class power levels, validation effectively covers the entire test ecosystem — package, cooling, and the test tools themselves, not just the device under test — because the test hardware becomes part of the system being qualified.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Implies test-equipment vendors now share reliability exposure with chipmakers at these power levels, and equipment specs (contacts, load boards, thermal control) become a gating factor for time-to-market.
insights.quote: At these kilowatt-class power levels, we’re essentially validating not only the device itself, but the entire package, the cooling, the test ecosystem itself,
insights.locator: That makes validation more than reproducing the rated power

insights.claim: Advantest says a kilowatt-class chip can enter thermal runaway within a few hundred microseconds, and test systems must detect the runaway condition via voltage drop across the contact and shut down before damage occurs.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Quantifies the sub-millisecond reaction-time bar test hardware must meet at 1kW, favoring more sophisticated ATE systems over legacy equipment.
insights.quote: A chip can go into thermal runaway within a few hundred microseconds,

insights.claim: Modus Test says sustained current heats test contacts over seconds, raising their resistance and limiting current-carrying capacity, with the same degradation occurring more slowly even under brief millisecond-duration pulses, meaning a contact can pass an initial continuity/opens-shorts test yet still fail once realistic current is applied.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Standard pass/fail continuity screening understates real-world test-contact failure risk at kilowatt power, a hidden yield-loss and cost driver in OSAT test operations.
insights.quote: As long as the pin is in contact with the PCB and the DUT, it may pass initial continuity, opens/shorts test, depending on the limits set in the test program,
insights.locator: A contact can therefore look healthy

insights.claim: Modus Test says current does not divide evenly across parallel power contacts because each contact has its own resistance; if several develop higher resistance, current concentrates through the remaining lower-resistance path, creating electrical overstress (EOS) that is catastrophic to the contact, socket, and device under test.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific failure mechanism — current hogging across test contacts — that can destroy both test hardware and the DUT, a cost/yield risk for OSATs qualifying kilowatt-class accelerators.
insights.quote: This will create what is referred to as EOS (electrical overstress) and is catastrophic to the contact, socket, and device under test.

insights.claim: NLM Photonics' CEO says OSATs cannot realistically exercise a kilowatt-class device long enough to guarantee long-term reliability — they run a basic burn-in and infer the structure 'should be fine' — because speed of delivery to customers takes priority over exhaustive qualification.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Flags a real gap between commercial delivery pressure and true reliability assurance for kilowatt AI accelerators; OSAT burn-in sign-off should be treated as necessary but insufficient evidence of long-run reliability.
insights.quote: OSATs do their basic test, do a burn-in and say, ‘Okay, yeah, we think the structure of this should be fine,’ but speed of delivery is critical. No one is going to run these systems ad infinitum to make sure that they live forever.
insights.locator: So how long can an OSAT realistically exercise

insights.claim: NLM Photonics says there is insufficient time and research funding to identify corner-case failure modes early, because AI GPU/CPU kilowatt-class device development cycles move faster than the engineering data needed to de-risk them can be gathered, with some data still being collected while the next design generation is already underway.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Implies the AI accelerator industry is structurally running ahead of its own reliability data, a systemic risk factor for anyone underwriting long-duration AI infrastructure reliability assumptions.
insights.quote: It’s very hard then to spend money on the research side to actually start pushing some of the technology and start finding the corner cases early,
insights.locator: There is still a point where the accelerator has to leave the lab

insights.claim: Nordson says the most concerning defects in kilowatt-class packages are not the large ones that cause immediate failure, but small defects — voiding, early delamination, interfacial cracking — that only cause operational problems after repeated thermal loading and cycling, and are often invisible in initial electrical test.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Makes the case for non-destructive inspection (acoustic, X-ray) before and after thermal stress cycles as a necessary step beyond electrical test, relevant to Nordson's addressable market in AI accelerator packaging QA.
insights.quote: The most concerning defects — the ones that will give you an operational problem down the line, particularly after a lot of thermal load and cycles — tend to be smaller defects,

insights.claim: Nordson says a large package can warp under thermal load and then relax back to its original shape as it cools, hiding the warpage from post-test inspection even though internal interfaces were already damaged during the stress event.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Shows that inspecting a cooled, at-rest package can miss real damage that occurred under load, implying test protocols increasingly need in-situ under-load inspection, not just post-test checks.
insights.quote: As soon as you remove that device from that situation, you take the heat away, you might lose that warpage,

themes.theme: Correlating Multi-Signal Telemetry Is The Hard Part

insights.claim: proteanTecs says chip timing margin is simultaneously affected by IR drop, temperature, process, and degradation, so no single measurement is meaningful in isolation — engineers need to correlate multiple moving signals against the actual workload and operating condition that produced them to separate real defects from normal variation.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Reinforces the market opportunity for multi-signal correlation and analytics platforms over point sensors in AI accelerator reliability monitoring.
insights.quote: It’s impacted by IR drop. It’s impacted by temperature. It’s impacted by process. It’s impacted by degradation.

insights.claim: Nordson says individual anomalies such as a small thermal excursion, marginal void, or timing shift may be benign alone but become predictive only when viewed statistically together as a trend across multiple parameters moving at once, reinforcing that failure prediction in kilowatt-class accelerators is a multivariate problem rather than a single-threshold check.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supports the investment thesis for AI-based predictive-maintenance and analytics tooling over simple threshold-alarm systems in semiconductor test.
insights.quote: It can be a combination of things that, statistically speaking, will point toward something that is going to happen later on. It’s finding those trends.
insights.locator: But individual measurements may not carry enough meaning

themes.theme: Validation Follows The Device Into The Field

insights.claim: proteanTecs says lab qualification cannot reproduce interactions between the chip, the system, and the data center that only appear after deployment, so some validation-grade visibility must follow the device into live operation, continuously collecting timing margin, IR drop, voltage droop, and cycle-to-cycle jitter data, not just voltage and temperature.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in reliability spend from one-time qualification toward continuous in-field telemetry, expanding the addressable market for silicon lifecycle monitoring vendors as AI accelerators scale to kilowatt power.
insights.quote: It’s not enough to collect voltage and temperature from the chip or from the system. You need to collect timing margin information, IR drop, voltage droop information, and cycle-to-cycle jitter.

themes.theme: The Ecosystem Has To Co-Design The Test Stack

insights.claim: Advantest says the industry historically treated the load board, tester, prober, and handler as separate systems, but at kilowatt wattages engineers now have to evaluate the full stack together, since the test hardware's own electrical and thermal behavior can shift the condition the device under test actually experiences.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Implies rising integration requirements across ATE, prober, and handler vendors serving AI accelerator test, a possible driver of tighter partnerships or consolidation.
insights.quote: Historically, we could separate the load board and the tester and the prober or the handler and kind of treat everything separately,
insights.locator: The full stack gets a vote

insights.claim: Teradyne says ATE vendors, handler/prober companies, and their cooling technology partners must now collaborate directly on a 'total solution' because advanced packaging thermal requirements are evolving faster than the test ecosystem can keep up with on its own.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signals that standalone ATE offerings are becoming less sufficient; partnership and integration across the test-equipment supply chain becomes a competitive differentiator.
insights.quote: It’s kind of like a three-way dance right now,
insights.locator: It's kind of like a three-way dance right now
